title: Heavy and light DNA in E. coli
body: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source was 15NH4Cl, so that all the DNA of the cells contained the heavy, non-radioactive isotope 15N. They then transferred the cells to a medium containing normal 14NH4Cl. E. coli divides once every 20 minutes. At definite time intervals they took samples, extracted the double-stranded DNA and separated it by centrifugation in a cesium chloride density gradient, where heavier DNA settles lower in the tube. After one generation in the 14N medium, all the DNA formed a single band of hybrid (intermediate) density. After the second generation, there were two bands of equal intensity: one hybrid and one light. The scientists compared these observations with what different models of replication would predict.

title: DNA evidence at a crime scene
body: A forensic laboratory received a blood stain from a crime scene and blood samples from two suspects, A and B. The DNA from each sample was isolated, digested with restriction endonucleases, separated by electrophoresis, blotted on to a nylon membrane and hybridised with a radiolabelled VNTR probe. The autoradiogram showed these bands (sizes in kb). Crime-scene stain: 2.1, 4.5, 6.0 and 9.3. Suspect A: 2.1, 3.8, 6.0 and 8.2. Suspect B: 2.1, 4.5, 6.0 and 9.3. During the investigation, the police also learnt that suspect B has a monozygotic (identical) twin who lives in the same town.
